title: CAP Theorem & PACELC
summary: The CAP theorem's real meaning under a network partition, why "CP vs AP" oversimplifies it, and the PACELC extension for the no-partition case.

slides.markdown:
The **CAP theorem** says a distributed system can't have perfect consistency, availability, and partition tolerance all at once — when the network splits, you must pick between staying consistent or staying available.

Most real systems can't skip partition tolerance (networks fail), so CAP really becomes: when a partition happens, does this system favor **C**onsistency or **A**vailability? **PACELC** extends the question to the normal case, when there's no partition. This topic gives you the precise version interviewers expect, not the oversimplified "pick two."

slides.sectionTitle: CAP theorem stated precisely: what C, A, P actually mean here
slides.markdown:
**Consistency** (in CAP, not the ACID sense) means every read receives the most recent write, or an error — no stale data, ever. **Availability** means every request to a non-failing node receives a response, though it might not be the latest value. **Partition tolerance** means the system keeps operating even when network messages between nodes are dropped or delayed.

The theorem, precisely: when a **partition** actually occurs, a distributed system must choose between consistency and availability — it cannot guarantee both for that duration. Outside a partition, this trade-off doesn't force itself on you at all.

slides.sectionTitle: Why you can't cheat CAP: an intuition/proof sketch
slides.markdown:
Picture two nodes, A and B, replicating the same value, with the network between them cut. A client writes a new value to node A. Now a client asks node B for that value.

Node B has two options: return its old, possibly stale value (choosing **availability** — it responds, but isn't consistent), or refuse to answer until it can confirm with A (choosing **consistency** — it's correct, but unavailable during the wait). There is no third option, because B genuinely cannot know A's latest value while the network is cut — this isn't an engineering limitation to be solved, it's what "partitioned" means.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a network partition forcing the C-vs-A choice
slides.markdown:
![A network partition forcing a choice between consistency and availability](assets/cap-partition.svg)

When the link between two data centers drops, each side keeps receiving client traffic but can no longer talk to the other. A **CP** system on the minority side refuses writes (or reads) until the partition heals. An **AP** system on both sides keeps serving, accepting that the two sides may now disagree.

The diagram is the whole theorem: the choice only exists *during* the partition — that's the trigger condition CAP is actually about.

assets.alt: A network partition forcing a choice between consistency and availability

slides.sectionTitle: CP systems vs AP systems: real examples
slides.markdown:
| System | Typical choice | Why |
|---|---|---|
| ZooKeeper, etcd | CP | Used for leader election / config — a stale answer could cause split-brain, so they refuse to answer rather than risk it |
| Cassandra, DynamoDB (default) | AP | Built for always-accepting writes; resolves conflicts later (last-write-wins or vector clocks) |
| Traditional RDBMS with sync replication | CP | A synchronous replica that can't confirm the write blocks it rather than risk data loss |
| DNS | AP | Stale records are tolerable; total unavailability of name resolution is not |

Most systems aren't purely one or the other — many let you tune the trade-off per operation (e.g., choosing quorum size in Cassandra).

slides.sectionTitle: The most common CAP misconception: "2 of 3, pick any two"
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "CAP means you pick any 2 of Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance, like a menu."

**Why it's wrong:** partition tolerance isn't optional for a real distributed system — networks *will* drop packets and links *will* fail, so "CA" (consistent and available, no partition tolerance) only describes a single-node system, not a distributed one. There's nothing to "choose" about P; it's a fact about networks, not a design decision.

**Correct model:** CAP is really a forced choice between C and A, and only *during* an actual partition. Phrase it that way in an interview and you'll immediately stand out from the "pick two" crowd.

slides.sectionTitle: PACELC: what happens when there's no partition
slides.markdown:
CAP only describes behavior *during* a partition — it says nothing about the normal case, which is most of the time. **PACELC** fills that gap: **if Partitioned**, choose **A**vailability or **C**onsistency (same as CAP); **Else** (normal operation), choose **L**atency or **C**onsistency.

That second half matters daily: a system can demand every replica confirm a write before acknowledging it (favoring consistency, at the cost of latency), or acknowledge as soon as one node has it and replicate asynchronously (favoring latency, at the cost of possibly reading stale data from another replica). PACELC is why "we chose AP" is an incomplete answer — it doesn't say what you optimize for on a normal Tuesday.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: PACELC classification of popular databases
slides.markdown:
| Database | Partition: A or C | Else: L or C |
|---|---|---|
| DynamoDB | AP | EL — favors low latency, eventual consistency by default |
| Cassandra | AP | EL — tunable per query, but defaults toward latency |
| MongoDB (default) | CP | EC — favors consistency even when not partitioned |
| Google Spanner | CP | EC — pays cross-region latency for strong consistency |

Naming a database's full PACELC classification (not just CAP) is a strong interview signal — it shows you understand the trade-off is live even when nothing is broken.

slides.sectionTitle: The staff-level nuance: CAP is a per-operation choice, not a per-system label
slides.markdown:
Labeling an entire database "AP" or "CP" is convenient shorthand, but the more precise truth is that many production systems make the C-vs-A choice **per request**, not once for the whole system. DynamoDB defaults to eventually consistent reads (AP-flavored, cheap and fast) but exposes an explicit `ConsistentRead=true` option per query that pays extra latency for a strongly consistent read from the current leader — the same database, offering both trade-offs, chosen call by call. Cassandra does the same with its per-query consistency level (`ONE` through `ALL`).

This means the honest interview answer to "is this database CP or AP" is often "it depends which operation, and what consistency level that specific call requested" — a single system can behave AP for one read path and CP for another, in the same deployment, at the same time.

The senior-level tell: an engineer who says "DynamoDB is AP" is quoting the default; one who adds "...but you can request a strongly consistent read on any query, trading latency for correctness where it matters" is describing the actual knob a real system gives you, not just its factory setting.
